content: The recommendations provided update the information regarding the influenza vaccine for the 1994-95 influenza season. These recommendations replace those published in the MMWR 1993;42(No. RR-6):1-13. Antiviral agents also play a significant role in controlling influenza. Introduction Influenza A viruses are classified into subtypes based on two surface antigens: hemagglutinin (H) and neuraminidase (N). Among influenza A viruses that have caused widespread human disease, three subtypes of hemagglutinin (H1, H2, and H3) and two subtypes of neuraminidase (N1 and N2) are recognized. Immunity to these antigens, particularly hemagglutinin, reduces the likelihood of infection and mitigates the severity of disease if infection occurs. However, infection with one subtype provides little or no protection against other subtypes. Over time, antigenic variation (antigenic drift) within a subtype can be so significant that infection or vaccination with one strain may not confer immunity to distantly related strains of the same subtype. Influenza B viruses exhibit greater antigenic stability than influenza A viruses, but antigenic variation still occurs. Consequently, major epidemics of respiratory disease caused by new influenza variants continue to occur. The antigenic characteristics of circulating strains guide the selection of virus strains included in each year’s vaccine. Typical influenza illness is characterized by the abrupt onset of fever, myalgia, sore throat, and nonproductive cough. Unlike other common respiratory illnesses, influenza can cause severe malaise lasting several days. More severe illness can occur if primary influenza pneumonia or secondary bacterial pneumonia develops. During influenza epidemics, high attack rates of acute illness lead to increased visits to physicians’ offices, walk-in clinics, and emergency rooms, as well as increased hospitalizations for lower respiratory tract complications. Elderly individuals and those with underlying health conditions are at increased risk for influenza-related complications. If they contract influenza, these high-risk individuals are more likely to require hospitalization compared to the general population. During major epidemics, hospitalization rates for high-risk individuals may increase twoto five-fold, depending on the age group. Previously healthy children and younger adults may also require hospitalization for influenza-related complications, but the relative increase in their hospitalization rates is less than that for high-risk groups. Increased mortality during influenza epidemics highlights the impact of the disease. Mortality increases not only from influenza and pneumonia but also from exacerbations of cardiopulmonary and other chronic diseases. During epidemics between 1977 and 1988, more than 40,000 influenza-associated deaths occurred during two of these epidemics. Approximately 90% of deaths attributed to pneumonia and influenza occurred among individuals aged 65 years or older. As the U.S. population ages and chronic diseases associated with aging become more prevalent, the number of deaths from influenza is expected to rise unless control measures are implemented more rigorously. The number of individuals under 65 years of age at increased risk for influenza-related complications is also growing due to improved survival rates for organ transplant recipients, advancements in neonatal intensive care, and better management of diseases such as cystic fibrosis and AIDS. Options for Influenza Control In the United States, two measures are available to reduce the impact of influenza: immunoprophylaxis with inactivated (killed-virus) vaccine and chemoprophylaxis or therapy with influenza-specific antiviral drugs (amantadine or rimantadine). Annual vaccination of high-risk individuals before the influenza season is the most effective measure for reducing the impact of influenza. Vaccination is highly cost-effective when directed at individuals most likely to experience complications or those at increased risk for exposure. Administering the vaccine during hospitalizations or routine health-care visits before the influenza season eliminates the need for special visits to physicians’ offices or clinics. Vaccination of residents in nursing homes and other chronic-care facilities can reduce the risk of outbreaks by inducing herd immunity. Inactivated Influenza Vaccine Each year’s influenza vaccine contains three virus strains (usually two type A and one type B) representing the influenza viruses likely to circulate in the United States during the upcoming winter. The vaccine is made from highly purified, egg-grown viruses that have been inactivated (rendered noninfectious). Influenza vaccine rarely causes systemic or febrile reactions. Whole-virus, subvirion, and purified-surface antigen preparations are available. To minimize febrile reactions, only subvirion or purified-surface-antigen preparations should be used for children; any of the preparations may be used for adults. Most vaccinated children and young adults develop high post-vaccination hemagglutination-inhibition antibody titers, which are protective against illness caused by strains similar to those in the vaccine or related variants that may emerge during outbreaks. Elderly individuals and those with certain chronic diseases may develop lower post-vaccination antibody titers than healthy young adults and may remain susceptible to influenza-related upper respiratory tract infection. However, even if such individuals develop influenza illness despite vaccination, the vaccine has been shown to prevent lower respiratory tract involvement or other secondary complications, thereby reducing the risk of hospitalization and death. The effectiveness of the influenza vaccine in preventing or attenuating illness varies, depending primarily on the age and immunocompetence of the vaccine recipient and the degree of similarity between the virus strains included in the vaccine and those circulating during the influenza season. When there is a good match between vaccine and circulating viruses, influenza vaccine has been shown to prevent illness in approximately 70% of healthy individuals under 65 years of age. Studies have also indicated that influenza vaccine is approximately 70% effective in preventing hospitalization for pneumonia and influenza among elderly individuals living in settings other than nursing homes or similar chronic-care facilities. Among elderly individuals residing in nursing homes, influenza vaccine is most effective in preventing severe illness, secondary complications, and death. Studies of this population have shown the vaccine to be 50%-60% effective in preventing hospitalization and pneumonia and 80% effective in preventing death, even though efficacy in preventing influenza illness may often be in the range of 30%-40% among the frail elderly. Achieving a high rate of vaccination among nursing home residents has been shown to reduce the spread of infection within a facility, thereby preventing disease through herd immunity. Recommendations for Influenza Vaccine Use Influenza vaccine is strongly recommended for any individual aged 6 months or older who, because of age or underlying medical conditions, is at increased risk for influenza-related complications. Health-care workers and others (including household members) in close contact with high-risk individuals should also be vaccinated. Additionally, influenza vaccine may be administered to any individual who wishes to reduce the chance of becoming infected with influenza. The trivalent influenza vaccine prepared for the 1994-95 season will include A/Texas/36/91-like (H1N1), A/Shandong/9/93-like (H3N2), and B/Panama/45/90-like hemagglutinin antigens. Annual vaccination with the current vaccine is necessary because immunity declines in the year following vaccination. Supplies of the 1993-94 vaccine should not be used to provide protection for the 1994-95 influenza season. Two doses administered at least one month apart may be required for satisfactory antibody responses among previously unvaccinated children under 9 years of age. However, studies with vaccines similar to those in current use have shown little or no improvement in antibody responses when a second dose is administered to adults during the same season.
